children: Kenya’s fresh produce exporters lost up to $3 million daily after aviation workers went on a go-slow this week, disrupting cargo operations at Kenyan airports and threatening shipments of flowers, fruits, vegetables, meat, herbs and spices to global markets.
The aviation workers union eventually reached a deal with the government to resume duty on Tuesday, but the three-day go-slow may have cost exporters a fortune already.
Industry players had also warned that any longer delays could damage the country’s reputation as a reliable supplier to international markets.
The Fresh Produce Consortium of Kenya (FPC) said the go-slow by airport and air traffic control workers was severely affecting the movement of perishable goods, causing huge losses.

FPC chief executive Okisegere Ojepat said exporters were losing an estimated $2 million to $3 million every day as flight and cargo operations were disrupted.“Every aircraft departing JKIA (Jomo Kenyatta International Airport) carries substantial quantities of Kenya's fresh produce, including flowers, fruits, vegetables, meat, herbs and spices, to markets across the world. This is cargo that cannot wait. When flights and cargo operations are disrupted, consignments miss connections, exporters lose money, orders are cancelled, produce risks deterioration and, ultimately, farmers, workers and the wider economy pay the price,” said Mr Ojepat.

The disruption came at a critical time for exporters who rely heavily on air freight to move high-value and highly perishable products to destinations in Europe, the Middle East and other international markets.

Mr Ojepat warned that the impact had gone beyond immediate financial losses and demanded certainty that future industrial actions do not hurt cargo exports.“More seriously, these disruptions are eroding the confidence of international buyers in Kenya as a reliable trading partner. We cannot afford to lose hard-won markets because our primary export gateway cannot guarantee predictable operations. This is not merely an airport inconvenience; it is an economic threat,” he said.

Kenyan aviation workers for the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, the regulator, the Kenya Airport Authority, which manages civilian airports in the country, and Jambojet, a subsidiary of Kenya Airways, had demanded improved welfare, better working conditions and the implementation of previously agreed employment benefits.
It was unclear if they had had all their demands addressed by Tuesday, but this strike had come after a previous deal was not honoured.
Stakeholders said delays had also affected other forms of logistics.
Hefty costsOgayo Ogambi, the CEO of Shippers Council of Eastern Africa (SCEA) said exporters also faced more costs for storage of cargo which should have left the country since Saturday last week.
The JKIA usually handles between 5,500 tonnes and 7,000 tonnes of cargo exports every week, consisting mostly of products that require careful handling and rapid transport.

According to Mr Ogambi, exporters are being charged between $0.10 and $0.20 per kilogramme per day for storage, adding another layer of costs to businesses already dealing with delayed shipments and possible losses from spoiled produce.“The exporters are experiencing huge losses, running into millions of shillings,” he said on Monday evening, hours before the strike was called off.
Going forward, these industry stakeholders said protecting the reliability of JKIA as Kenya’s main international air cargo gateway will be essential to safeguarding the entire value chain.
